description: Payer-behaviour matrix (#169). Each row is one legal or illegal payer behaviour, run end to end through OnboardingRunner by PayerMatrixTest. The expected verdict and findings come from the cited spec clause, not from what the workbench currently reports. A row the workbench gets wrong today names its issue in knownDefect; the test then requires the mismatch, so fixing the defect fails the row until the marker is removed.

legend.auth: The connection's authType. NONE and OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS run against NorthwindPayer, CDS_HOOKS_JWT against FabrikamPayer, OAUTH2_PRIVATE_KEY_JWT against TailspinPayer, each configured with this row's PayerBehaviour.
legend.behaviour: PayerBehaviour fields; anything left out keeps the standard behaviour; tokenType OMITTED leaves token_type out of the response. clockOffsetSeconds moves the payer's clock and its Date header. redirect.to is same-host (a path on the same payer) or other-host (a second loopback server that counts what reaches it).
legend.expect.verdict: RunVerdict status: PASS, PASS_WITH_WARNINGS or FAIL.
legend.expect.findings: Check id to the most severe finding expected from that check (FAIL > WARN > INFO > PASS), or ABSENT when the check must report nothing.
legend.expect.brokeAt: The first failed step, when the row expects one.
legend.expect.otherHostUntouched: The other-host redirect target received no request at all.

rows.clause: An access token is a string representing an authorization issued to the client. The string is usually opaque to the client.
The client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token ... The OAuth 2.0 framework assumes that access tokens are treated as opaque by clients.
The client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token: the authorization server and the resource server might decide to change the token format at any time.

The resource server MUST validate that the aud claim contains a resource indicator value corresponding to an identifier the resource server expects for itself (§4). That obligation is the payer's: the client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token (§6), so a payer that accepts its own token with another aud gives the client nothing to report.
The sizes of tokens and other values received from the authorization server are left undefined. The client should avoid making assumptions about value sizes.

rows.spec: RFC 6749 §5.1; SMART Backend Services (STU 2.2) access token response
rows.clause: token_type: REQUIRED. The type of the token issued as described in Section 7.1. Value is case insensitive. SMART fixes the value as "bearer".
token_type: REQUIRED. The type of the token issued as described in Section 7.1. Value is case insensitive.

token_type: REQUIRED. A response without it leaves the client unable to tell what type the token is. §7.1: The client MUST NOT use an access token if it does not understand the token type. The router SDK sends every token as Bearer, so auth.token warns that the type is missing.

§7.1: The client MUST NOT use an access token if it does not understand the token type. A DPoP-bound token needs a proof on each request, which the router SDK does not send: it sends every token as Bearer. auth.token warns that the type is not Bearer.

§7.1: The client MUST NOT use an access token if it does not understand the token type. A mac token is signed per request, which the router SDK does not do: it sends every token as Bearer. auth.token warns that the type is not Bearer.

Parameter names and string values are included as JSON strings. Numerical values are included as JSON numbers. A numeric string such as "300" is non-conforming, but the router SDK accepts a numeric-string expires_in, keeps the 24 h cap, and caches nothing else (owner decision on #177), so the lifetime is usable and auth.token passes with a note.

Numerical values are included as JSON numbers. A string that is not a number of seconds ("5 minutes") is no lifetime at all: the router SDK caches nothing but a positive number or numeric string, so it treats the token as having no expires_in, which auth.token warns about.

expires_in: The lifetime in seconds of the access token. A fraction (3599.9) is not the positive whole number of seconds #177 accepts, so auth.token warns; the router SDK reads a JSON number with Jackson's asLong(), which truncates it, so it caches the token for 3599 s, and the warning must say so.
The client MUST ignore unrecognized value names in the response.

RFC 6749's own example response carries Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8. RFC 8259: No "charset" parameter is defined for this registration. Adding one really has no effect on compliant recipients.

A successful response carries access_token (REQUIRED) with a 200 status; an error is answered with HTTP 400 (unless specified otherwise) and an error parameter. A 200 carrying only error and error_description issued no token.

CDS Services SHOULD require authentication if invoking the service poses any risk of exposing sensitive data to the caller. A service that requires none is legal, and an unauthenticated hook call to it must succeed.

The client can request an access token using only its client credentials. The authorization server MUST support the HTTP Basic authentication scheme for authenticating clients that were issued a client password.

Each time a CDS Client transmits a request to a CDS Service which requires authentication, the request MUST include an Authorization header presenting the JWT as a Bearer token. For CDS Hooks, this [aud] value MUST be the URL of the CDS Service endpoint being invoked. Authentication raises nothing; the one warning is FabrikamPayer's own CRD 2.0.1 coverage-information form (the RI's identifier sub-extension), which response.coverage-information reports on every Fabrikam run.

rows.spec: SMART App Launch STU 2.2, Client Authentication: Asymmetric; RFC 7523 §2.2
rows.clause: exp: This time SHALL be no more than five minutes in the future. jti: A nonce string value that uniquely identifies this authentication JWT. iss and sub are the client_id; aud is the token endpoint URL.

rows.spec: RFC 6750 §2.1; CDS Hooks 2.0, Trusting CDS Clients
rows.clause: Clients SHOULD make authenticated requests with a bearer token using the Authorization request header field. Whether the resource server checks it is the server's decision (CDS Services SHOULD require authentication); the client did its part and the call succeeded.

If the protected resource request does not include authentication credentials or does not contain an access token that enables access to the protected resource, the resource server MUST include the HTTP WWW-Authenticate response header field. The payer answers 401; the run must fail and say no credential was sent.

rows.spec: CDS Hooks 2.0, Trusting CDS Clients; RFC 7519 §4.1.4
rows.clause: exp: Expiration time integer for this authentication JWT. The processing of the exp claim requires that the current date/time MUST be before the expiration date/time. The client signs exp five minutes after iat, so a payer clock five minutes ahead sees it expired and rejects it: a rejection consistent with clock skew.

Implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew. iat identifies the time at which the JWT was issued. The payer accepts a JWT issued five minutes in its future; a stricter payer would not, so the run passes with a clock-skew warning.

The processing of the exp claim requires that the current date/time MUST be before the expiration date/time listed in the exp claim. An hour of skew is far past any leeway; the rejection is caused by the clocks.
iat: identifies the time at which the JWT was issued. This payer checks only exp, so it accepts a JWT issued an hour in its future; the measured offset is far beyond tolerance and must be reported.

rows.spec: SMART App Launch STU 2.2, Client Authentication: Asymmetric; RFC 7523 §3
rows.clause: The JWT MUST contain an exp (expiration time) claim that limits the time window during which the JWT can be used. The authorization server MUST reject any JWT with an expiration time that has passed. Five minutes of payer skew expires the five-minute assertion.

rows.spec: SMART App Launch STU 2.2, Client Authentication: Asymmetric
rows.clause: exp: This time SHALL be no more than five minutes in the future. By a payer clock five minutes behind, the assertion's exp is ten minutes ahead, so the payer rejects it.
The authorization server MUST reject any JWT with an expiration time that has passed, subject to allowable clock skew between systems.

rows.spec: SMART App Launch STU 2.2, Client Authentication: Asymmetric
rows.clause: exp: This time SHALL be no more than five minutes in the future. RFC 7523 §3: the authorization server may reject JWTs with an exp claim value that is unreasonably far in the future. An hour of payer skew puts exp more than an hour ahead.

The client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token, so the token's skewed iat and exp are not the client's to judge; client_secret_basic carries no time claim. The payer validates against its own clock and accepts, so nothing measurable is skewed.
expires_in: The lifetime in seconds of the access token. A lifetime is relative, so a skewed payer clock does not change it, and client_secret_basic sends no time claim to compare.

The user agent MAY use the Location field value for automatic redirection (following is optional), and since the redirection can change over time, the client ought to continue using the original target URI. The Discovery endpoint SHALL always be available at {baseUrl}/cds-services, so a redirect there means the connection record is wrong and must be reported.

rows.spec: RFC 9110 §15.4; CDS Hooks 2.0, Trusting CDS Services
rows.clause: Automatic redirection needs to be done with care. Each CDS Client vendor/provider SHOULD maintain an allow list of the CDS Services it has vetted. The workbench's endpoint guard (#138) only calls the approved payer host, so nothing may reach the other host.

Automatic redirection needs to be done with care for methods not known to be safe; the token request is a POST carrying the client secret. Following is optional (MAY), so the token step reports the redirect instead.

A user agent following a redirect removes Authorization, and automatic redirection of unsafe methods needs care. The client secret is for the authorization server the client registered with, so the redirected token request must not reach the other host.
The response to the discovery endpoint SHALL be an object containing a list of CDS Services. Each CDS Service SHALL be described by hook, description and id (REQUIRED).

rows.spec: CDS Hooks 2.0, Discovery; CDS Hooks 2.0, Extensions
rows.clause: Discovery lists every CDS Service the server hosts, whatever its hook. The specification reserves the name extension, allowing implementations to use it to provide custom behavior. A client picks the services for the hooks it calls.
prefetch: OPTIONAL. An object containing key/value pairs of FHIR queries that this service is requesting the CDS Client to perform.
If your CDS server hosts no CDS Services, the discovery endpoint should return a 200 HTTP response with an empty array of services. Legal, but there is no order-sign service to onboard against.
